articles.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
articles.summary: Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort
body: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation.

The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians.

According to the project, some 283 Indonesians were recruited in the first nine months of this year to fight for Russia against Ukraine. It said recruitment from Indonesia was no more than 10 in the previous three years.
Related: ‘I made the biggest mistake’: the young Yemeni men lured into the Russian army with empty promises
The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions about the alleged recruitment effort but it is not the first time Russia has sought foreign mercenaries for its war effort.
In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia.

A growing number of people from African countries – including Kenya, Uganda and South Africa – and elsewhere have been lured to the frontline as Russia seeks help to sustain its more than four-year war after invading Ukraine in February 2022.
This month Jakarta urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians were drafted into its military, following the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military.

Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang said: “The Indonesian government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure that no Indonesians will be recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues.”
Indonesia, she added, was particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking.
Days later, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting its nationals that used social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The posts promised lucrative jobs in logistics, border security and defence construction, but after the applicants travelled to Russia they were directed to sign contracts to serve as mercenaries, with some deployed to conflict zones, police said.

The ‘I Want to Live’ governmental initiative was established in September 2022 by the coordination headquarters for Prisoners of War with support from Ukraine defence ministry and defence intelligence (HUR).
It was designed to allow active-duty troops, including Russian servicemen and foreign nationals recruited into the Russian military, to safely surrender and exit the battlefield.

articles.title: Fresh concerns raised over Gaza doctor held by Israel for 23 months without charge
articles.summary: Independent Israeli professor says Hussam Abu Safiya’s life will be at risk until he receives proper medical treatment
body: An independent professor who reviewed the medical records of a prominent Gaza doctor held in an Israeli prison without charge for nearly 23 months has raised serious concerns about his health.
Hussam Abu Safiya was detained at work on 27 December 2024 and later held in solitary confinement at Rakefet, a notorious underground prison.

During a visit by a lawyer from Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) in the summer, the doctor told of harsh conditions, untreated medical problems and severe food shortages. Witnesses said he had become almost unrecognisable.
Nearly 700 days after his arrest, Israeli authorities have yet to bring any formal charges against Abu Safiya, who is the director of Kamal Adwan hospital in northern Gaza.
He was classified as an “unlawful combatant” along with more than 375 medical workers – a designation Israel has used to justify prolonged detention without trial.

Last month, Israel’s supreme court rejected a petition to release the doctor. Over the weekend, a district court rejected a separate petition to allow Abu Safiya an independent medical examination, despite troubling findings in his medical records that were not adequately investigated, according to Prof Amit Tirosh, an independent Israeli specialist who reviewed a file obtained by PHRI.
In an interview with the Guardian, Tirosh said Abu Safiya’s weight had fallen from 90kg (14st 2lb) in January 2025 to 76kg this May.
“Continuous food deprivation and weight loss, repeated beatings and injuries, with inadequate medical care, can definitely cost Dr Abu Safiya his life,” Tirosh said.
“According to PHRI records, more than 100 prisoners died in Israeli facilities between 2023 and 2025 … a threat to his life unfortunately cannot be ruled out.”
Tirosh identified insufficient investigation of chest pain, delays in treating scabies and a drop in haemoglobin levels that warranted further examination.

“A 14kg weight loss is very alarming, even more so if the cause is unknown,” he added. “More troubling, the medical team was neither surprised nor concerned: one prison physician wrote that his weight loss over a year is ‘a common trend among security prisoners associated to their diet’.
“Haemoglobin dropped between February and July 2026, long after the weight loss, so detention or starvation alone cannot explain it; it coincided with the reported beatings in Rakefet.
“Such blood loss can be life-threatening and requires urgent ER evaluation. Per the records, these urgent problems were not addressed and could endanger his life.”

Medical records documented bruising around one of Abu Safiya’s eyes, dizziness and rib pain in July. He told his lawyers he had been beaten by prison guards but Tirosh said the records did not explain his injuries.

The district court ruling also revealed allegations made by Israeli authorities that Abu Safiya had exaggerated his medical problems, set up organisations from prison, influenced other prisoners and maintained international contacts.
PHRI said the Israeli allegations did not justify denying him an independent medical examination, a right protected by law.
“The bottom line is that a third party should see him and the full medical records,” said Tirosh. ‘‘Refusing an independent examination is never justified.

“To the Israeli prison system authorities I would say that I feel deep shame to be counted with them as a doctor or health provider in Israel. As a system, they betray every medical and ethical principle I stand for.”
The Israeli prison service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Abu Safiya had become the face of health workers struggling to treat patients throughout the war in Gaza before his detention. He is being held indefinitely, along with thousands of other Palestinian civilians, in prisons that Israeli rights groups say have become torture camps.
At the time of his arrest at work, Abu Safiya was wearing a white medical coat that he had refused to wash since his son, Ibrahim, was killed by a drone strike at the hospital entrance that October.
Abu Safiya had helped keep the hospital running through more than 80 days of siege and attacks by Israeli forces amid an intensive military operation in the surrounding refugee camp.

“Fourteen Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, remain imprisoned without charge or trial at a time when Gaza’s healthcare system desperately needs them,” said Naji Abbas of PHRI.

A spokesperson for the Israeli prison service (IPS) told the Guardian the allegations are “part of a broader campaign aimed at discrediting the state of Israel” and that the IPS “operates in accordance with the law and under constant judicial oversight”.
Abu Safiya’s family have not been able to communicate with him directly in detention.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Putin ‘lives in a different reality’ as Abu Dhabi talks get under way
articles.summary: Ukrainian president dismisses Moscow’s claims of gains in Donbas region but says first day of trilateral talks were constructive. What we know on day 1,722
body: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has backed Ukraine’s assessment of what is happening on the battlefield and that Vladimir Putin lives in a “different reality”, as American-led trilateral discussions between Ukraine, ⁠Russia and the US got under way in Abu Dhabi. In a post on social media, Zelenskyy said that Russia has claimed at the talks that they occupied half of the Donbas in Ukraine’s east. “This is the problem. Putin lives in a different reality,” the Ukrainian president wrote, adding “I can draw a picture for him too where I fully occupy Russia. But it’s not true. What was good is that the American side confirmed the Ukrainian assessment of what is happening on the battlefield.”

Zelenskyy said he was “happy” to see a change in the approach by US mediators at the Abu Dhabi talks. “I see changes. I’m very happy with what I hear. We will see what can be done,” Zelenskyy told a press conference in Copenhagen after being asked about changes in the approach to peace talks made by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.

Zelenskyy described the first day of talks – the first three-sided discussions to be held since February – as constructive and substantive. He said the agenda in Abu Dhabi had included formulating a new security architecture for Europe, an idea raised earlier on Tuesday by Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We are all very cautious with this topic because nobody really understands 100% what they want. I think we understand, but nobody ​saw the documents, what the Americans discussed with the Russians,” Zelenskyy said.

In Abu Dhabi, US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war, Andrew Roth and Jennifer Rankin report. Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said, but European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence.

Ukraine’s foreign minister said he ⁠had urged US secretary of state Marco Rubio to accelerate ⁠interceptor ​deliveries as Russia ramps up attacks on energy ⁠infrastructure. Speaking to Reuters after talks ​with Rubio, Andrii Sybiha said he had pressed Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow even as diplomatic efforts to end the war took ‌place in Abu Dhabi. He said Ukraine remained prepared to ​discuss a range of de-escalatory measures, including ceasefires covering the Black Sea and energy infrastructure.

Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month, Jennifer Rankin reports from Brussels. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister, Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava, alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš.

A drone attack sparked a fire at a key Russian port for oil exports, the regional governor announced. “A UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack hit the port area of Ust-Luga, causing a fire,” Aleksandr Drozdenko posted on Telegram, referring to one of Russia’s most important western oil hubs that has been repeatedly attacked by Ukraine. Teams were working to extinguish the fire, he added.

Latvia ⁠and Lithuania warned people across several regions to take shelter due ⁠to threats ⁠of ​unidentified drones entering their airspace via neighbouring Russia or Belarus early on Wednesday. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said its warning included ⁠the country’s second city of Kaunas, which has ​a population of about ‌300,000 people. As ‌Ukraine attacks Russia’s Baltic Sea oil shipping ports, some of its drones have ​missed their targets and led to security warnings in neighbouring countries. Moscow ⁠has accused Kyiv of using Nato airspace ​as cover ​for attacks, while Kyiv ​says some of its drones have ​been steered off ‌course by Russian ​signal ​jamming. The Nato countries blame Russia for the incidents, saying it ignited the war.

articles.title: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron file new defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens
articles.summary: Legal battle escalates as far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man
body: Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron have brought a fresh defamation lawsuit against Candace Owens in her home state of Tennessee, in an escalation of a transatlantic legal battle as the far-right US podcaster continues to spread false claims that France’s first lady was born a man.

The Macrons first sued Owens and her media companies in July 2025 in Delaware in response to what the French first couple called “verifiably false and devastating lies” being repeated by Owens on her podcast and on X. According to that lawsuit, those lies included that Brigitte Macron, 73, was born a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her older brother – and committed identity theft to hide a gender transition; that Emmanuel Macron was elected as French president as part of a CIA mind-control program; and that the couple are blood-related relatives committing incest.

A judge ruled that the Macrons’ claim was limited in scope to Owens’s companies registered in Delaware after she successfully argued that the court’s jurisdiction did not extend to her personally as she did not live in that state. The case against her companies remains pending.

Meanwhile, the new lawsuit filed on 4 November in Nashville, Tennessee, where Owens resides, includes 88 counts of defamation, false light and defamation by implication. They are against Owens personally and build on the Macrons’ original demand for punitive damages against the podcaster on the grounds that she has persisted with the false claims.

“Mrs Owens was adamant that Tennessee is where this case belongs because it’s where she lives,” a representative for the Macrons’ legal team said. “With this filing, we are giving her exactly what she has repeatedly demanded.”

The new complaint stated that since the Delaware lawsuit was filed, Owens had “unequivocally doubled down”, publishing further “outlandish, defamatory, and far-fetched fictions” through her eight-part podcast series called “Becoming Brigitte” – along with accompanying posts on X.

The filing also alleges that Owens – who has millions of followers across her podcast and social media channels – has a financial motive in continuing to peddle the false claims. “She has continued to use her podcast to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her ‘reporting’ on the Macrons,” the complaint says.

The new lawsuit mentions a “Brigitte doll” that Owens holds in her videos, describing it as “a grotesque, alien-like figure” that is reminiscent of the namesake character in the fictional film ET. The doll “caricatures Mrs Macron’s body”, the lawsuit contends, while adding that Owens’s use of the doll confirms “that her campaign against Mrs Macron is driven by animus toward Mrs Macron’s perceived gender identity, gender, and sexuality”.

The French first couple has experienced “relentless bullying on a worldwide scale” as a result, the lawsuit alleges. It says: “Defendant has subjected the Macrons to a campaign of global humiliation, turning their lives into fodder for profit-driven lies. Owens has dissected their appearance, their marriage, their friends, their family, and their personal history – twisting it all into a grotesque narrative designed to inflame and degrade.”
The Macrons are seeking actual, presumed and punitive damages, in addition to a narrowly tailored injunction barring Owens from republishing any defamatory statements.

“To be clear, there is nothing shameful or defamatory about being a man, being transgender, or being gay,” the lawsuit says. “Owens’ statements are defamatory because they accuse the Macrons of lying to France and to the world, for decades, about who Mrs. Macron is – and of committing crimes to conceal that supposed lie.”

The Guardian has contacted Owens for comment. On X, she wrote in part: “The Macrons have indeed filed a NEW set of claims against me. 88 in total, and this time, they want justice over my Brigitte-Doll.
“Those of you who are fans of the show know that Brigitte-Doll has never pursued the limelight. For her to be called ‘grotesque’ by the French couple is hurtful, to say to the least.
“Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.”

articles.title: French police raid Ritz hotel in Mohamed Al Fayed sexual abuse investigation
articles.summary: Arrests made after three properties were searched in relation to inquiry into late businessman
body: French police have made arrests after raiding three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, in relation to an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking by Mohamed Al Fayed.

Several individuals were taken into custody for questioning last month and later released, according to the Paris public prosecutor’s office. Another property in Paris and one in Saint-Tropez, both with links to Fayed, were also searched in mid-October.
Several of Fayed’s alleged victims were also interviewed by officers from the organised crime division of the Paris prosecutor’s office.

It added that the searches were part of a preliminary investigation into “allegations of human trafficking committed by an organised group, aggravated pimping committed by an organised group, and rape”.

In an email sent to survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse earlier today, the Metropolitan police said its officers were present during the searches on 13 and 14 October, in a coordinated operation with French investigators.

The Paris prosecutor’s office said: “Searches and evidence-gathering operations were carried out in mid-October 2026, notably within the Hotel Ritz in the 1st arrondissement of Paris, as well as at the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, a former property of Mohamed Al Fayed, and at the Villa Windsor in the 16th arrondissement of Paris, in the presence of British investigators.”
The investigation is ongoing and digital material seized during the searches is being analysed, it added.

One of the properties that was raided was Castel Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez, one of the most exclusive villas on the French Riviera, and where Diana, Princess of Wales, stayed with her sons in the summer of 1997, at the start of her relationship with Fayed’s son, Dodi.

The other was Villa Windsor, a former holiday home of the Fayed family. The property in western Paris was previously the family home of Charles de Gaulle, before he was president of France, and King Edward VIII, after his abdication, and his wife, Wallis Simpson.
A Met spokesperson confirmed its officers travelled to France last month and were present during the operation.
Campaign groups representing Fayed’s alleged victims called on the Met police to conduct its own searches of the late billionaire’s properties.

Co-chairs of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, said: “We want to see the same thoroughness applied to every property where survivors say they were taken or abused, including here in Britain. The searches in Paris and Saint-Tropez must be the beginning, not the end.”

A spokesperson for No One Above, a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said: “The French authorities have put this in the hands of their specialist trafficking unit and their organised crime prosecutors, and are investigating it as trafficking by an organised gang.

“The evidence in this case was never confined to Harrods. For two years, the Met has avoided treating it as what France recognised from the outset: organised trafficking by a network. The National Crime Agency should now take over the investigation.”

Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she was overjoyed by the French police raids. “Survivors deserve actions, not words,” she added.

Last November, she told French investigators from the Central Office for the Repression of Human Trafficking that Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of €65,000 a year if she slept with him.

Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 169 victims who have contacted the force directly.

The Ritz Paris told Agence France-Presse news agency that it “does not tolerate any form of harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour” and that it was ready “to cooperate fully with the competent judicial authorities”.

articles.title: Israeli opposition hurries to seize control as new Knesset is sworn in
articles.summary: Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has mandate to try to form a government – with Netanyahu waiting if he fails
body: Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they fail to broker a coalition.

Priorities include setting up a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks and introducing term limits for Israel’s prime ministers, which could block Netanyahu from taking power again. He has ruled Israel for 19 of the last 30 years.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, now has the presidential mandate to try to form a government. If he fails to broker a deal within six weeks, a second candidate – probably Netanyahu – will get a second chance. Further failure is likely to lead to another election.

Netanyahu responded to the swearing in of the new Knesset on Tuesday with a racist attack on two Palestinian-led opposition parties, whose voters were essential to unseating his coalition, calling their lawmakers “terror supporters”.
Eisenkot denounced his speech as a “delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful” exploitation of a state occasion, that showed the prime minister was unfit for office.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, and Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish-Israeli former police chief who ran on the slate of Islamist Ra’am party, both walked out of Netanyahu’s speech in protest.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the country’s population. Netanyahu put attacks on these voters and their parties at the heart of his campaign, and since polling day has promoted groundless accusations of fraud in their communities in a bid to undermine results.
Election officials say there was no evidence of irregularities that affected the election outcome or compromised its integrity.

A period of prolonged, difficult coalition negotiations or even a new round of elections would extend Netanyahu’s hold on power as caretaker prime minister. But if the fractured opposition can make progress on key legislation, his grip on the state would be weakened.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party submitted a series of bills to the Knesset moments after the swearing in, with backing from other opposition parties.

In addition to term limits and the 7 October inquiry, legislation includes several bills designed to revoke the “judicial overhaul” pursued by Netanyahu, which weakened the power of Israel’s judiciary and the attorney general.
Ohana has tabled the vote on a new speaker to replace him for next Tuesday, the latest date possible. The opposition have also nominated candidates to take over key defence and finance committees.

Eisenkot has admitted the path to power is “extraordinarily complex”, because of incompatible election promises made by different parties, but described ousting Netanyahu as a national emergency that could require breaking promises.
At the swearing-in ceremony, the president, Isaac Herzog, warned lawmakers they should do everything in their power to avoid a second election.

“Reach out a hand for compromise, even between ⁠rivals … Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House.“

articles.title: Activist wins 10-year fight against homophobic Trinidad and Tobago laws
articles.summary: Jason Jones welcomes decision by privy council in London to overturn 2025 ruling that outlawed anal sex
body: A gay man has won a historic 10-year battle against Trinidad and Tobago’s homophobic laws with a landmark UK appeals court ruling that could help overturn similar anti-gay laws in other Caribbean countries.

The privy council, based in London, overturned a 2025 decision by Trinidad and Tobago’s court of appeal that recriminalised consensual anal sex, seven years after the Trinidadian activist Jason Jones secured a high court judgment declaring the country’s colonial-era “buggery” laws unconstitutional.

Delivering the ruling, the privy council judge Lord Sales said: “The ability to form a deep connection with another person through an intimate and loving relationship is a vital interest for all human beings.”

The privy council is the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago and several other Commonwealth countries, giving the ruling potentially far-reaching significance for other Caribbean jurisdictions where similar laws remain in force.
“This judgment will have a domino effect across every country that has the privy council as its supreme court. It will change many millions of people’s lives,” Jones said in a statement.
“I’m looking forward to going home, switching off everything and living with this moment for a while.”

In an interview after Tuesday’s hearing, he added: “We may not see the benefits of this for 50 years. What a judgment says in a courtroom and what happens in your home and workplace are two entirely different things.
“I don’t focus on changing hearts and minds. I have done this for my community, for our hearts and minds, so that we can stand proudly and at least say we are not criminals.”

The LGBTQ+ rights activist Peter Tatchell, who was also at the courthouse, said: “There will certainly be LGBT people and human rights defenders in at least a dozen countries who will now use this privy council judgment to push for decriminalisation in their home countries. It sets an absolute gold standard for decriminalisation.”

Jones’s lawyer, Caroline Edwards, hailed Tuesday’s unanimous victory as “an emphatic victory for Jason, for all gay men and women in Trinidad and Tobago and for all people who believe in the fundamental rights of everyone”.

Reflecting on the case’s long journey, she said: “All judges who heard the case in Trinidad and Tobago were unanimous that the 1986 legislation was not justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for rights and freedoms, and all the privy council judges agreed.”

Jones has been fighting the “buggery law”, introduced in 1925 under British colonial rule, since 2016, arguing that it violated his constitutional rights. His case hinged on whether the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were protected by the “savings clause”, which shields certain older laws inherited from the UK at independence from being struck down as unconstitutional.

In a historic 2018 victory, the high court judge Devindra Rampersad ruled that the provisions criminalising consensual anal sex were unconstitutional. But the government appealed and last year won a ruling reversing that decision after the court of appeal found the provisions were protected by the savings clause.

Tuesday’s privy council decision backed Rampersad’s original ruling, with all five judges finding that parliament’s 1986 Sexual Offences Act amounted to new legislation rather than merely a continuation of colonial-era laws and therefore could not be protected from constitutional challenge by the savings clause.

The privy council also upheld Rampersad’s remedy that makes anal sex legal between consenting adults of any gender over the age of 16. It also decriminalises same-sex intimacy, referred to in the archaic 1925 act as “gross indecency”.

Jones’s court case is the latest significant victory for LGBTQ+ rights in the Caribbean. It follows a landmark ruling in St Lucia last year, when the Eastern Caribbean supreme court struck down colonial-era laws criminalising consensual gay sex.
Jeshua Bardoo, a lawyer and founder of Equal Rights, Access and Opportunities St Vincent and the Grenadines, described Tuesday’s decision as a “historic moment for LGBTQ+ rights”.

“Unfortunately, in my country, SVG, a high court judge upheld these laws as constitutional in 2024. I believe that this decision will be very persuasive to the case currently under way or future litigation in SVG, as privy council decisions are usually binding on lower courts,” he said.

Joel Simpson, the founder of the Society Against Sexual Orientation Discrimination, a Guyanese LGBTQ rights organisation, described the ruling as a “monumental victory for LGBTQIA+ people in Trinidad and Tobago and across the Caribbean”.

“This ruling is another powerful sign of the growing momentum across the Caribbean to leave behind outdated colonial-era laws that criminalise people simply because of who they are and who they love,” he said.

Téa Braun, the chief executive of the Human Dignity Trust, said there was hope the case signalled a continuing regional trend of tackling “antiquated laws” that “violate the human rights of LGBTQ+ people”.

“This issue continues to be litigated in domestic courts across the region, and we hope the trend – which began with a judgment in Belize in 2016 and was followed by Antigua, Barbados, St Kitts, Dominica and St Lucia – will continue,” she said.
In Trinidad and Tobago, Pride TT welcomed the ruling as a “significant moment in Trinidad and Tobago’s journey towards equality”, but said it did not mean the struggle for LGBTQ+ people was over.
“We must acknowledge that the removal of these discriminatory provisions does not mean that all the challenges facing LGBTQIA+ people have suddenly disappeared,” it said.
“Discrimination, stigma, exclusion and unequal treatment remain realities in many aspects of everyday life, including employment, education, housing, healthcare and access to public services.”

Asked whether this would make Jones, who has lived in London for several decades, feel comfortable living in Trinidad again, he said no. “The thing about liberation movements is every time you move the needle forward, you get the pushback. I got a lot of pushback from the queer community [in Trinidad], saying: ‘Don’t stir the pot.’ But you have to. I’m not afraid of pushback.”

articles.title: US officials seek ‘final end’ to Russia-Ukraine war, as Abu Dhabi talks set to continue
articles.summary: First substantive peace talks since February include US proposal for ‘long-term security architecture’ between Moscow and Europe
body: US officials have said they are seeking a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine as trilateral talks got under way in Abu Dhabi, the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.

The talks, which are set to go into a planned second day on Wednesday, are also the first since the US launched joint strikes with Israel against Iran, and they follow bruising midterm elections that have weakened Donald Trump at home.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who like Vladimir Putin was not in Abu Dhabi, described the discussions on the first day as “constructive and fairly substantive”.
“We discussed in detail the substance of security guarantees for Ukraine and the foundations for their long-term implementation,” he said in a social media post.
Part of the Trump administration’s proposal involves drawing up a new “long-term security architecture” between Russia and Europe, administration officials have said.

European officials are concerned that Russia may stick to its hardline demands that Nato should roll back its military footprint across eastern Europe, which would threaten to leave allies vulnerable to Moscow’s influence at a time of historic tensions with the west.

European officials held separate discussions on Tuesday with representatives from Ukraine and the US, where they agreed “any future arrangements must respect sovereignty, territorial integrity, independent decision-making, and provide credible security guarantees for Ukraine”, according to a joint statement.

European leaders are not convinced Russia intends to negotiate in good faith and want to be involved in discussions, although there are signs of unease about the proliferating strands of peace talks. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, last week complained about the “disorderly” process of meetings and phone calls that, she argued, weakened Europe’s ability to speak with one voice.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Tuesday it was a goal at some point to expand the Russia-US-Ukraine talks to include other European voices.

“There’s always this concern in Europe that they’re going to be left out, that America’s going to cut some deal with Russia and leave Europe out of the equation. Well, Europe’s at the table. They’re with us,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Paris, speaking after the UAE talks had finished for the day.

Since his first decade in power, Putin has complained about Nato’s eastward expansion and sought to renegotiate the balance of power between Nato and Russia – but never before have those demands been embraced by a sitting US administration, which has made it clear that it is desperate to get to a deal.

Previewing the discussions, a US administration official said the US would “need Europe at the table” to end the war. He said negotiators could also revive the Nato-Russian council that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and potentially lift sanctions against Russia to get to a deal.

The US officials also claimed that they had discussed with Russia potential security guarantees to Ukraine similar to Nato’s article 5, which protects member states in case of an attack. Russia has strongly opposed Nato admitting Ukraine or western countries placing troops in Ukraine.
“What they would be getting would be effectively very similar to Nato,” an administration official said.

“Getting a US security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” the official added, saying it would be up to Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Zelenskyy to discuss. “And if he wants to do that, that’s a very, very big deal in terms of resources and funding and military support.”

Critics have expressed scepticism about what may trigger those security guarantees, however, noting that article 5 does not oblige Nato member states to defend others, and that cyber-attacks and other forms of hybrid warfare have blurred the line for what would require a military response.

Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a lead negotiator for the US, described a potential new framework for Europe in general terms on Monday, saying the US would seek “stronger consultation, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, and reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, while fully respecting the sovereignty and independent decision-making of every nation”.
A European security official said that the US proposal was not yet clear and that they were bracing themselves for the US to pose serious concessions to Russia during the Abu Dhabi consultations.

The EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, told a G7 foreign ministers meeting on Monday: “We already have a European security architecture in place. This includes international agreements under which Russia has undertaken obligations, including with regard to sovereignty and territorial integrity. The problem is that Russia is not respecting these agreements.”
Trump has also said that Ukraine would probably be expected to give up territory in a final deal, and would end with a “little bit different shape”.

After meeting the Kremlin adviser Kirill Dmitriev last week, Trump said he would seek a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”. Critics are concerned that Trump and Putin could try to go over the heads of European leaders in order to negotiate a peace that gives serious concessions to Russia.

“There’s a lot of baggage that people in Europe have about this idea,” said a US administration official, pointing specifically to Russia’s 2021 proposal that was viewed as an ultimatum to Nato to get out of eastern Europe.

At that time, Russia issued a list of demands to Nato that included a ban on expansion to new countries including Ukraine, a rollback of troops to its pre-1997 borders, and limits on where it could place missiles. Nato rejected that proposal, and Russia invaded Ukraine less than a month later.

The US administration official said: “We have to build something new that works today … Because if all the old architecture was working well, then we wouldn’t be in this long war. And so obviously something’s not working, and we need to come up with a way that when we end this war, it really is a final end to the war.”

articles.title: Merz accused of ‘blackmail’ by Slovak PM after demand for Ukraine aid in EU budget
articles.summary: German chancellor has signalled he will block budget with no aid deal, complaining that burden is ‘carried mostly by only a few member states’
body: Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month.

The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort.
“What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister, Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava.

He was speaking alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, whose populist government also rejects taking part in a future loan for Ukraine. “I do not know why he is saying it,” Babiš said, referring to Merz’s position.

Merz wants EU leaders to discuss Ukraine’s financing needs at a summit in Dublin on Friday. “We must continue to support Ukraine in its fight to defend itself. This is in our shared vital interest,” he wrote in a letter, seen by the Guardian, to the European Council president, António Costa, who will chair the meeting. “And yet, bilateral assistance to Ukraine is distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states.”

The EU last year agreed to lend Ukraine €90bn, which was intended to cover two-thirds of its military and civilian costs for 2026 and 2027. But since then, Russia’s relentless bombardment has heaped more costs on Kyiv, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to call for €70bn to fill a budget shortfall.
The EU has endorsed Zelenskyy’s figures and pledged to find €45bn, with Ukraine’s other allies, such as the UK and Canada, expected to provide the rest.
Merz last year led an effort to use Russia’s €210bn sovereign wealth frozen in the EU, but the plan was scuppered by opposition led by Belgium, which hosts most of the funds at Brussels.

The €90bn loan was the fallback plan. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia, which opted out of that loan, have indicated they will stay out of the next round. Those three member states have now been joined by Bulgaria, following the election of Moscow-friendly prime minister Rumen Radev last April.

The issue of Ukraine’s financing is now ricocheting into tortuous negotiations on the EU budget for 2028-34. Germany, the largest net contributor, wants steep cuts in the proposed budget, while opposing generous EU funding for member states that refuse to chip in to Ukraine’s financial needs.

In his letter Merz writes that “a collective commitment … without exception” is an “essential pre-requisite” for resolving Ukraine’s funding shortfall and “discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications”.

He also states that all member states need to contribute to a “sound” financial perspective for Ukraine from 2028 in the context of the EU’s next seven-year budget, known as the multiannual financial framework.
A German government official said: “Financial support for Ukraine of all EU member states is essential in order to successfully complete the MFF.”
Berlin is also seeking to switch the decision-making process on funding Ukraine to a qualified-majority vote, rather than unanimity, in order to prevent one government from blocking EU decisions.

The letter reflects growing exasperation from the EU’s northern member states that are Ukraine’s most generous backers over smaller contributions from other EU member states in central and southern Europe.

The task of finding an agreement on the budget falls to Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister. He wants a deal by the end of the year, before elections in France, Poland and Italy in 2027 that are likely to complicate the task.

A spokesperson for Costa confirmed receipt of the letter without commenting on details. “President Costa will make time for interventions on Ukraine at the informal European Council in Dublin this week,” the spokesperson said, adding that Ukraine finance would be discussed at a special summit dedicated to the EU budget on 26-27 November.

articles.title: Singapore seizes US-operated cruise ship that offered ‘permanent’ life at sea
articles.summary: MV Odyssey impounded by authorities almost a fortnight after passengers left stranded in Cambodian port
body: Singapore has seized a US-operated cruise ship that offered retirees a “permanent” life at sea but instead offloaded them in Cambodia after it ran out of money due to soaring fuel prices.
After more than 200 passengers were left stranded in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville last month, the MV Odyssey sailed on to ⁠Singapore last week and has been impounded by authorities.

“The vessel has been placed under arrest ⁠pursuant to a court order,” Singapore’s Maritime and Port ​Authority said in ‌a statement. “The crew onboard ‌are reported to be well and arrangements for their ‌welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel’s creditors. There are no passengers on board.”

According to court records, ​the MV Odyssey was listed “under sheriff’s arrest” on Sunday morning ​just off Singapore’s east coast, meaning it had been detained but was not necessarily under any criminal charges.
Related: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare

It was not clear why the ship had been impounded, although Singapore is a global shipping hub, and it is not unusual for ships facing commercial issues to relocate to the city-state to resolve disputes.
The local Straits Times reported that the ship’s Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, owed approximately US$500,000 in fuel payments. Villa Vie Residences has been contacted for comment.

On 27 October, and with only a few hours’ notice, the company disembarked all passengers, saying fuel ⁠price surges from the Iran war had made operations ​“unsustainable”. Mikael Petterson, the founder ‌and executive chair of Villa Vie Residences, later said the ship was now being operated by creditors.
Most of the passengers of the MV Odyssey were Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials said.

Passengers were sold what the company website said was “a new model of global living at sea”, with the 195-metre (640-ft) vessel offering multi-year residencies as well as permanent cabin costs between $120,000 (£90,000) and $440,000. However, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, the company said in a statement.

Some passengers have stayed in Cambodia to assess their options, including Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who had been documenting their life at sea on YouTube. In a video published last week and filmed on a beach with the Odyssey in the background, the couple said the “bank” was now making a decision on its fate. They later filmed the ship leaving at night.

The round-the-world cruise faced issues from the start, including a four-month delay in setting sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024. Several passengers reported signs of financial distress during the cruise, including accounts of guests raising extra money for fuel.

Randy Cassingham, a writer living onboard the ship, said after passengers were off-loaded, residents had also passed a jar around to raise $100 each for lower-ranking crew. He said few passengers expected to recover any of the funds they had spent on their cabins, as they knew the company had “been in terrible money problems from the beginning”.

articles.title: Viktor Orbán’s brother detained in people-smuggling investigation, Hungarian PM says
articles.summary: Arrest made by anti-corruption body set up to investigate alleged graft during former PM’s 16-year rule
body: Hungarian authorities have detained a brother of Viktor Orbán as part of an investigation into people-smuggling, the prime minister, Péter Magyar, has said.

The Hungarian anti-graft body, the national asset protection and recovery office, said in ⁠a statement that a joint operation with police had led to the arrests of four people and searches of homes in Budapest and Pest county.
While the statement did not name the three men and one woman who had been detained, Magyar linked one of the arrests to the former prime minister.

“Three ex-ministers of Orbán are already in custody,” Magyar said in Berlin, where he gave a speech on Monday evening. “Already his brother today ⁠went to custody,” he added, referring to the former leader’s sibling Aron Orbán, 49.

In April, Magyar won a landslide election victory, ousting Orbán after 16 years in power during which the country slumped in rankings to become the most corrupt in the EU. In the leadup to the vote, Magyar crisscrossed Hungary vowing to investigate any allegations of corruption and abuses of office that had taken place during his rival’s rule.

On Monday, as news broke of his brother’s arrest, Viktor Orbán accused officials of carrying out a “political witch-hunt”, in a post on social media. “The aim of this dirty political game is to eliminate opponents and establish a one-party state. I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me,” said Orbán, who remains president of his rightwing nationalist Fidesz party.

Shortly after taking power in May, Magyar set up the national asset protection and recovery office, an independent body with a mandate to uncover any past abuses of public funds and prevent future violations. He described the office as a central plank of a wider anti-graft campaign that he called “Operation Purgatory”.

Magyar has alleged that corruption, including the misuse of public funds, may have cost Hungarians as much as 10% of the country’s gross domestic product in recent years. Orbán has denied all allegations of wrongdoing.

Police said in a statement on Monday that the four people detained were suspected of helping Vietnamese citizens reach western Europe for several months in 2024. The timeline suggests the alleged activities took place while Orbán was still in office.

The perpetrators were accused of assisting more than 100 Vietnamese citizens in obtaining visas at Hungary’s foreign missions in Vietnam, in exchange for a ⁠ recruitment fee which they then shared, the authorities said.
The four detained are suspected “of human smuggling committed as part of a criminal conspiracy for the purpose of financial ‌gain”, police added.
One of the suspects is alleged to have engaged in influence peddling during the process of acquiring visas.
The arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile police actions against former officials or other individuals linked to the former prime minister.

In the months since Orbán lost power, three former ministers from his government have been taken into custody over graft accusations in separate cases, including the former central bank governor György Matolcsy. All have denied any wrongdoing.

When contacted by the Guardian on Tuesday, the lawyer representing Aron Orbán declined to comment. She referred instead to an earlier interview she had given to Hungarian media in which she said there was no basis for the arrest.
With contributions from Reuters and Associated Press

articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh from exile
articles.summary: Former prime minister faces death penalty upon return after being sentenced in absentia over deaths in 2024 uprising
body: Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister applied for a new passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She crossed the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.
Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.
Related: The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from India

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had already returned in anticipation.

On Monday, a British lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina wrote to the Bangladesh high commission in Delhi requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges against her and claimed the tribunal that convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, the Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government, which was close to Hasina while she was in power, has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.
This week, the Bangladesh government said that, as a “terrorist”, Hasina would only be allowed to return via an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty.
Aminul Islam, the chief prosecutor of the tribunal that sentenced Hasina, said there was “no legal scope” for her to be issued a new passport as she was a “convicted fugitive”.

Islam emphasised that Hasina would be hanged if she returned, as the deadline for her to appeal against her conviction had passed. “Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” he said.

Despite the abuses and oppression that mired her 15 years in power and subsequent conviction for crimes against humanity, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many of whom have been driven underground.

Analysts said they believed her decision to return was driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly elected government, led by Tarique Rahman. It came to power in February during Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
The government has since struggled with inflation and protests that shut down garment factories, which the Awami League hopes to use to its advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite many of them facing serious criminal charges and having been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is based in India.

Some senior party figures have returned in recent months, including the former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. He was immediately arrested on his return in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder during the 2024 uprising.
Exiled Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.
Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press: “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people.”

articles.title: ‘We are human too’: the Roma film-makers striking back at stereotypes
articles.summary: Seven films in Seville programme highlight how Roma are creating their own narratives
body: Growing up in Romania, whenever Alina Șerban spotted Roma people on television or in movies, they were usually cast as villains or depicted as somehow exotic.

But this week the Romany actor and film-maker is part of a cohort pushing back against this stereotyping, joining forces with Romany film-makers from across Europe in a landmark screening of seven films during the Seville European film festival.
“It’s work made by us, not just about us,” said Șerban. “I was raised in a world where everything I heard about my community came from the exterior … The perspective is finally being centred.”

Her film, I Matter, which tells the story of a young woman who reckons with her Romany identity as she comes of age, was screened earlier this year as part of the Venice film festival’s spotlight section, where it won the audience award.

It was a triumph for a film that Șerban had envisioned as a way to build bridges towards “a different understanding” of Romany people, who rank among Europe’s most marginalised communities, with longstanding discrimination leading to challenges in accessing decent housing and the segregation of children in schools.
“I wanted to show, in a very simple but complex manner, that we are human too,” she said. “I’m claiming Roma humanity.”

Organisers described this week’s showcase, titled Raising Romani Gaze and housed within the wider Seville festival, as the first of its kind. “This is something that we have been building up to for around 10 years,” said Katalin Bársony, a Romany film-maker from Hungary and one of the curators of the programme.

The wide range of talent in the community as well as a willingness in the industry to recognise their narratives had made it possible now. “Romany people, despite being the biggest minority in Europe, we are one of the most underserved and invisible when it comes to our own art that we create,” said Bársony, who also leads the Romédia Foundation, an NGO which seeks to use storytelling, film and visual archives to strengthen Roma self-representation and challenge prejudices.

The result was a programme that offered an unprecedented glimpse of Europe’s richness by giving “narrative sovereignty” to some of the estimated 10-12 million Roma who live across Europe, she said. “From the start of the silent film, Romany people have been put in certain roles. And those roles were mostly passive and defined by the outside gaze.”

The films range from a documentary by Bársony that follows a young man born in Germany to Roma parents and who is deported to Kosovo, to a film by the Spanish director Jero de los Santos that delves into queer and Romany perspectives.

The showcase also includes Smooth the Edges, by the Nottingham-based Romany film-maker Charles Newland. “It’s a bit of an outlier,” said Newland, “because it’s the first film funded by the British Film Institute by a Romany director with a Romany producer and a lead Romany cast.”

The short captures a dilemma that Newland described as common in Britain’s Romany community: that of a young woman who wrestles with whether to hide her background in order to avoid workplace discrimination. What emerges is the tension in the trade-off of being able to escape discrimination but at a cost of repressing part of herself. The film also sought to engage with the in-between world that Roma in the UK were often forced to reckon with, said Newland.

“Especially politically, there are a lot of people who can be racist against my group of people, but then on the same token, when it suits their argument, refer to you as white as well,” he said. “Sort of like, ‘oh they’re just Gypsies, they’re scum’ when it suits that agenda, but if it’s an agenda of trying to help out, it’s like, ‘well, why do they need help because they’re just white people?’ So you get stuck between this rock and a hard place.”

By bringing together Roma film-makers from across Europe, this week’s programme also offers a chance to push back against what has unfortunately become a common thread in the lives of many Roma across the continent, said Șerban. “As they say, the last form of acceptable racism is towards Roma people,” she said. “Being Roma for me, at least in the Romanian context, and for my generation, meant that you were somehow inferior.”

Against that backdrop, every decision she took on her film felt like an “act of resistance”, she said. “Hopefully, in some years’ time, there will be 50 or 100 films like mine. But since I was one of the first to bring this perspective, I had all this pressure and all these nuances to think about. You become an ambassador without choosing to be one.”

She saw it as a necessary step, however, in seizing the chance to tell stories that could allow audiences to see Roma living complex human experiences while also allowing Roma to see themselves on screen as more than just stereotypes. “Films bring change,” she said. “Art makes people think of how life is for another person.”
The Raising Romani Gaze programme will run at the 23rd Seville European film festival from 10 to 14 November 2026

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: The world is falling short on climate action. Can Cop31 change that?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: As global leaders gather in Turkey for the UN climate summit, both doubts and hope surround what the annual talks can achieve
body: Good morning. After another year of unprecedented droughts, floods and wildfires driven by human-caused global heating, 91 heads of government will meet tomorrow in Turkey to discuss the climate crisis. They will do so against a backdrop of global instability and conflict.

But as high-ranking officials and civil society campaigners settle in for a fortnight of speeches, protests and labyrinthine negotiations at the UN’s 31st annual climate conference, Cop31, many are asking what the point is.

Those same governments pledged more than a decade ago in Paris, at Cop21, to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels, but implementation has been sclerotic, and only two months ago a UN report warned temperatures will reach at least 1.8C using even the most optimistic future projections.

I spoke to the Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey in Turkey about what’s on the Cop31 agenda, what success looks like and why Brazil’s re-elected president Lula will be the star of the conference.
UK | Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”.

US | Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Russia | US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.
Technology | Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.
Climate | Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
The 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change – or Cop31 – is taking place in the Turkish coastal city of Antalya until 20 November.

The conference centre – which, as at every Cop meeting, is temporarily designated UN international territory and policed by UN security officers – is set on the outskirts of the city. At this time of year, it is usually the venue for a global conference of plastic surgeons, part of a billion-dollar industry in Turkey.

But this week and next it will host an estimated 70,000 registered delegates, from the professional lanyard class to civil society campaigners. When we spoke at lunchtime, Fiona had already spotted Indigenous groups from the Amazon, Australia and the Pacific in national dress – a colourful sight at every Cop, where indigenous delegates know they can attract significant media attention.

When I reported with Fiona from Cop26 in Glasgow, five years ago, inclusivity was a major theme, with observers from Indigenous communities, trade unions and environmental NGOs complained that they had not been given sufficient access to formal negotiating spaces, and staged a symbolic walkout on the final day.

This is a long-running argument, says Fiona, alongside running questions about the scope for campaigners to host protests and alternative gatherings around the conference venue. “Four out of five of the last Cops were held in countries with repressive regimes,” she reminds me, where scope for outside dissent was very limited.

Annual Cop summits rotate between countries from different regions of the world, but this year a rancorous dispute between Turkey and Australia has resulted in an unhappy compromise. Turkey is the official host and in charge of the action agenda, the “jolly bits” that surround the voluntary agreements, rather than the tension of formal negotiations.

Australia is in charge of those, which will see countries thrash out the details of just transition and climate finance programmes. This is “the short straw” says Fiona, with none of the pleasing global focus of physical hosting, and with climate advocates questioning Australia’s credibility to manage these negotiations as a major fossil fuel producer. Although Turkey is hardly a better fit: as Fiona puts it, “The one thing they have in common is their mutual admiration for coal.”

Formal negotiations this year will mainly be focused on the just transition mechanism, which aims to ensure people who are working in fossil fuel industries aren’t completely abandoned in the move to renewable energy, as well as helping poorer countries - who happen to be significantly less responsible for the climate crisis – to access enough finance to deal with the worsening climate crisis.

This year, Fiona has sensed less urgency from global leaders over Cop31. Alongside the anticipated absence of the Trump White House, as well as China’s Xi Jinping and India’s Narendra Modi, there are some other disappointing no-shows. The UK’s Andy Burnham is due to arrive, alongside the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen, but the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor Friedrich Mertz will not attend, nor will Canada’s Mark Carney.

Fiona also questions whether the Cop process is fit for purpose. “The negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris ‘rulebook’ under which the treaty is put into effect. And the convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given petrostates free rein to obstruct progress,” she says.

But Fiona, a Cop optimist, says there are two places where progress can be made. The first is through the informal discussions, known as the action agenda, which generate voluntary commitments alongside the binding commitments under Paris. The second, the part of the formal negotiations known as the “cover decision”. Some of the “really dynamite” advances from previous Cops can be found in this text – such as the agreement to transition away from fossil fuels, which every single country signed up to at last year’s Cop30 in Brazil. This year, Brazil’s president, Lula, is expected to bring a plan for how to make that happen.***
What could be achieved at this year’s conference?

The UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the Paris agreement overshoot and bring down global temperatures by the end of this century. This can’t happen without a transition away from fossil fuels and the Brazilian delegation is bringing a detailed global roadmap for how this can be done – though it won’t be part of the formal negotiations..

While the Brazil roadmap does not include a timetable for phasing out fossil fuels, it is still an important contribution as it sets out the different dilemmas that countries face – such as losing tax revenues by cutting fossil fuel use, for instance, or axing subsidies which might have helped poorer households. “This means governments can recognise the issues they will face in their transition, as well as the benefits, and plan accordingly,” says Fiona.

The talks will also seek support for a new 2035 electrification goal, backed by Turkey and Australia, under which 35% of final energy use around the world coming from electricity instead of fossil fuels.

This comes as China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year, in part owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles, with many other countries following suit – but not the UK it seems. As we reported exclusively yesterday, ministers are expected to make steep cuts to the government’s EV targets – their biggest decarbonisation policy – in a move that will alarm many Labour MPs who are concerned about the government’s commitment to the green agenda and may be embarrassing for Burnham as he flies into a conference with electrification so high on the agenda. Some experts argue that the inbuilt efficiency of electric tech compared with fossil fuels means that a global switch to electrification would halve energy demand around the world.

China – still one of the world’s biggest polluters – is dominating energy transition with some astonishing results: its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal, saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars. And solar is booming in Africa at last, adds Fiona.

The re-election of President Lula has buoyed climate activists everywhere, who take hope from his success in beating far-right populism with an unashamedly climate-focused agenda, which aims to secure the vitally important Amazon rainforest for future generations.
This is his first international trip since last month’s electoral triumph, and Fiona predicts he’ll receive “a stupendous welcome.”

His presence is also important as a vocal champion of climate justice. “He says very clearly it’s the elites, of both developed and developing nations, who are responsible for the biggest emissions with their high carbon lifestyles and investments in fossil fuel companies, not the ordinary people”.

We’ll likely hear more from him about his proposals for a potentially transformative global wealth tax – at previous international summits Brazil has argued for a 2% tax on those with assets worth more than $1bn. “He wants the people who have benefited from this to pay. It’s a hugely powerful message. How can you argue against that?”

I loved Stephen Phelan’s interview with Jorge Drexler – a Uruguayan medic who grew up under an anti-music dictatorship and went on to write an Oscar-winning song. “‘Predator’ Brand sentenced to 10 years for rape and sexual assaults”, is the Guardian’s splash today. The Times and the i Paper both have “Brand jailed for 10 years”, the Mirror writes “10 years”, and the Express also has “Sex predator Brand jailed for 10 years”. The Mail says “Brand facing more claims”, the Telegraph writes “Goldsmith: Brand abused me”, the Sun has “Still no remorse”, and Metro says “not so funny now, are you Russell?”.
Elsewhere, the FT leads on “Nvidia shares fall as board investigates Huang’s exposure to China spy claims”.
Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years in jail

Russell Brand, once an award-winning comedian and Hollywood actor, has been sentenced to more than 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault. The judge paid tribute to the “determination and bravery” of the women who came forward in the case, and described Brand as a sexual predator of “staggering arrogance”. Police are investigating two further additional rape allegations and have urged all rape and sexual assault victims to report what happened, “no matter how long ago it occurred”. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Last month, the Student List group ousted Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia’s elections, and young people helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s Presidential victory against the rightwing Flávio Bolsonaro. Meanwhile, students in France, Spain and Germany have recently protested against unacceptable school conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living respectively.Research suggests that youth-led protests tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others. But these young people will not be cowed.“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion [are] tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
