articles.title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM
articles.summary: Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government
body: Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.

High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda and committee chairs. The current speaker is Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.

He will be replaced by Matan Kahana, from the Yashar party led by Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military chief who got the presidential mandate to try to form a coalition government at the weekend.

Kahana, a former minister, fighter pilot and special forces officer, has the explicit backing of all four Jewish Israeli parties in Eisenkot’s “change” bloc. The two other Palestinian-led opposition parties have said replacing Ohana is a priority so are expected to give Kahana their votes.

The opposition parties hold 67 seats in the 120-seat legislature, enough to install a consensus choice for speaker. They will request a vote on Tuesday afternoon, and Ohana then has up to a week to bring it to the floor.

Avigdor Lieberman, who heads another opposition party, is nominated to head the foreign affairs and defence committee. It will play a central role in drawing up planned legislation covering the conscription of ultra-Orthodox men, a key campaign issue for Lieberman.

The effort to wrest away control of the Knesset is significant enough that more than 160 former top security officials, including heads of the military, intelligence and police, warned at the weekend that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the day with violent attacks.

“Actors who oppose replacing the Knesset speaker intend to go to the Knesset on the day of the swearing-in ceremony and to prevent the MKs and their family members from entering the building,” a forum of retired commanders said in a letter to serving security chiefs.
“These same actors are encouraging tens of thousands of citizens who support their stance to come and to help them with their mission,” Ma’ariv newspaper quoted the letter as saying.
All opposition parties have described Netanyahu as a threat to the state and are keen to start moving against him in the Knesset, despite divides blocking the formation of a coalition.

Several of the Jewish-Israeli opposition parties in Eisenkot’s bloc have sworn not to sit with the Palestinian-led parties, which hold more than a quarter of the bloc’s seats, or even join a minority government that has their backing.
Eisenkot has vowed to broker a national emergency government, promising to achieve it with “creative and unconventional political acts”.

In a sign of challenges ahead, he effectively warned that some election promises would have to be broken to unseat Netanyahu. “No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise. That is also leadership, to know when to decide and set priorities,” he said.
There have been protests across Israel urging Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to put unseating Netanyahu ahead of a racist commitment to excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the population and voted in unprecedented numbers this year, giving the parties 19 seats. Without them, the opposition bloc would have fewer seats than Netanyahu’s diminished coalition.
Lieberman has been trying to seek an alternative path to government through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties.

They have long been Netanyahu allies but have been frustrated by his failure to deliver on the promise to pass broad military draft exemptions for their community into law. Lieberman has campaigned hard for universal conscription, but appears to prefer compromise on this issue to working with Palestinians.
“Has the End of Times arrived?” the leading Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) journalist Arye Erlich wrote in a column for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.

“Has Avigdor Lieberman … the biggest persecutor of Haredim Israeli politics has seen in decades, suddenly come to believe that he can compromise on a military draft bill and sit in a coalition government alongside the Haredim?”

Even if Eisenkot does broker a coalition deal, he may delay announcing it until Netanyahu’s speaker has been replaced. Netanyahu is a master of political survival and last-minute deals, fracturing past coalitions by luring defectors into his own alliance.
Ohana could delay signing in a new government for up to a week, and some of the opposition do not want to give Netanyahu that much time to attack the pressure points of any fragile deal.

If Eisenkot cannot form a government, the mandate is passed to other leaders, and if they fail, Israel must hold elections again. In the meantime Netanyahu and his far-right allies would stay on as a caretaker government.
Although Netanyahu is calling for his opponents to join him in a unity government, a long period of limbo followed by a new vote offers him a likelier path back to power.
If an alternative government took power, it would be harder for Netanyahu to destabilise it, said Gideon Rahat, a chair in political science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Once they establish a government, they might be a minority government, it might be hard for them to do things, but nevertheless, they will be governing and it would be hard to oust them.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: battlefield gains bolstering Kyiv’s hand in US-led peace talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Ukrainian president says battlefield successes and mounting Russian losses add to negotiating leverage ahead of Abu Dhabi talks on Tuesday. What we know on day 1,721
body: Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy has said ⁠that ​battlefield ‌successes ‌were strengthening Kyiv’s position ‌in negotiations, on ⁠the ⁠eve of ​new US-led trilateral talks ⁠on resolving the war. “Every ​task that is fully accomplished, every ⁠defensive operation that increases ​Ukraine’s strength ​and ​delivers results, strengthens ​Ukraine ‌and, above ​all, ​strengthens us in negotiations,” the president said in his nightly video address on Monday. Zelenskyy said ​top Ukrainian military commander Mykhailo Drapatyi had presented ‌a report that underscored heavy recent losses by Russian forces. He added that Ukraine’s long-range strikes on ‌Russian targets, including oil industry sites, were also working.

Russia’s battlefield losses have reached levels unprecedented in its modern history, according to data shared with the Guardian’s Pjotr Sauer. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine over nearly five years of fighting, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat. The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, shows 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.

US negotiators in Tuesday’s Abu Dhabi talks believe that Zelenskyy and Russian president Vladimir Putin may be willing to strike a compromise on ‌the vital question of territory, with each ceding a little, an American official told Reuters. Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to accession to the EU. In a 60 Minutes interview broadcast on Sunday, Donald Trump said Ukraine would have “a little bit different shape” under the settlement, but he didn’t elaborate. A senior Ukrainian official strongly denied that the government would consider any such concessions.

Trump on Monday said that Washington was seeing ​a “very strong inclination” towards ending the war and that both sides were “tired of fighting.” However, US secretary of state Marco Rubio gave a more sober assessment of peace efforts. Rubio said the process still has “ways to go”, and that getting Europeans to the table with the Russians has still not happened. “It’s been difficult to get anything productive out of that,” Rubio told reporters a day before the talks.

European powers, ⁠including France, Germany and the European Commission, ⁠will send officials to the talks, but Russia has made it clear it doesn’t want the Europeans to take part in negotiations. Instead, Ukrainian delegates will meet separately to brief their European allies on progress. “We are doing everything to ensure that Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process,” Rustem Umerov, the head of the Ukrainian delegation, said on Monday.

EU foreign ministers pressed Rubio at a G7 meeting in Paris to ensure Europe is represented at the negotiations. German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said after talks with Rubio: “Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe – only with Europe.” Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said on Monday that Trump’s team had placed “collective security”, covering not just Russia and Ukraine but also a wider area, at the top of the agenda.

Russian forces targeted four electrical substations in Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, Russia’s defence ministry said Monday. The attacks are part of Russia’s campaign to deny Ukrainian civilians heating, light and running water during the approaching winter. Zelenskyy said Monday the EU had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power grid repairs. Russian forces also hit a warehouse in Odesa in south-western Ukraine containing food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said.

A long-range Ukranian drone attack started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest, close to St. Petersburg, Leningrad governor Alexander Drozdenko said on Monday. Ukrainian forces also struck a plant near St. Petersburg, Russia’s second-largest city, that produces solid rocket propellant for Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Ukraine’s general staff said.

articles.title: Witnesses recount struggle to save people buried in ‘horrifying’ Gaza landslide
articles.summary: High winds and heavy rain triggered collapse of sand bank overlooking camp for displaced families
body: Witnesses have described the frantic struggle to save three members of a family buried by a landslide triggered by high winds and heavy rain in Gaza.
A sand bank overlooking a camp for displaced families south of Deir al-Balah collapsed on Sunday, killing five people and crushing at least three tents.

“It was a horrifying sight,” said Abdul Karim al-Sahhar, 30, originally from Izbat Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza. “We saw people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. Even the tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”
Among the casualties were an eight-year-old, a six-year-old and their mother.

Sahhar, whose own shelter was badly damaged in the landslide, said the children’s father was outside the family tent and so survived. “One of his children had called him to come and eat with them,” he said. “He was a little late returning, and then the collapse happened.

“The father started shouting: ‘Save my children! Save my children!’ People came and started digging [but] there was a huge boulder on top of the victims. The young men had to break it into pieces so they could reach the people buried underneath.”

Abu Darbali, another witness, said the collapse of the embankment sounded like an explosion. “We found that three tents were covered completely after the mountain collapsed on top of them,” he told Reuters. “People were under the rubble and we couldn’t see them.”
Video posted to social media showed people using hammers to break large rocks and others removing sand with shovels, using flashlights to search for those trapped underneath.
The UN said more than 26,000 households had reported damage to shelters or belongings after the weekend’s rainstorms.

The vast majority of Gaza’s population of 2.3 million live in tent encampments or the ruins of bombed-out buildings, ‌with reconstruction yet to begin after Israel’s relentless two-year military assault launched after the Hamas attacks on southern Israel in October 2023.

“The collapse [this weekend] was waiting to happen. [Gaza] is extremely overcrowded. People are just trying to find a place wherever,” said Toby Fricker, a spokesperson for Unicef, which has been working to prevent similar tragedies and improve drainage in camps for displaced people.

In a statement, the Hamas-run government media office said about “70,000 tents sheltering tens of thousands of displaced people were flooded on the first day” of rains. It also noted the “collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs, which caused injuries”, some critical, in various areas of the tiny territory.

A US-brokered ceasefire last year called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory ‌from which residents have been ordered to leave.
Israel says no reconstruction can happen before Hamas is disarmed.

Sahhar said he and his family were now homeless. “My tent and everything I own are now buried under the sand. My mattress, household utensils and all my belongings – everything was buried. I could not retrieve anything,” he said.

Mustafa Qazzaat, a member of the Gaza City council, said Israel had not allowed prefabricated homes to shelter the displaced since the truce was announced, and only permitted the entry of limited numbers of tents.
Many so-called “dual use” items remain restricted, such as metal tent poles. Humanitarian workers said they instead had used wooden poles fashioned from palettes used to transport food.

Cogat, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees aid to Gaza, said more than 91,000 tents and over 8,200 trucks containing tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had reached Gaza, as well as convoys carrying supplies of fuel and engine oil to power pumping facilities and other humanitarian installations.

Earlier this year, an assessment compiled by shelter specialists in Gaza revealed that thousands of tents supplied by China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia to shelter displaced Palestinians offered only limited protection against rain and wind.

articles.title: ‘I know what it’s like to fight’- France’s most popular sportsman says he’s running for president
articles.summary: Five-times Olympic judo champion Teddy Riner says he is neither leftwing nor rightwing but would seek to ‘bring people together’
body: The French judo star and five-times Olympic gold medallist Teddy Riner has announced plans to run in next year’s presidential election, describing himself as someone neither leftwing nor rightwing but who would seek to “bring people together”.

With more than five months before the April-May ballot to replace Emmanuel Macron, the race has been shaping up to be a showdown between political extremes. Polls point to a hollowing out of the political centre, suggesting that the anti-immigrant National Rally leader Marine Le Pen could be the frontrunner, with the radical-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon trailing behind.
Riner joins a crowded field of candidates, with analysts describing him as a long shot, given his lack of experience and no party backing.
On Monday, he sought to position himself as someone who would unite people and bring “common sense, steadfastness, justice” to France.
“I know what people are going to say about me: ‘He’s crazy. He’s not from the establishment. He doesn’t have the codes. He’s never done politics,’” Riner said in a video posted on social media.

He listed the issues facing the country, from soaring debt to the rising cost of groceries and the precarious futures faced by those who don’t have the right network, family name or skin colour. “If refusing to bow my head and refusing the chaos makes me crazy, then yes, I’m completely crazy,” he said.

The announcement comes about six weeks after Riner, who has often been voted France’s most popular sportsperson, faced a wave of racist abuse and online harassment after telling a TV sports show he felt “anxiety” about the rise of the far right in France.
It also comes as the country has been rocked by protests over the cost of living, heightening the ongoing protests by schoolchildren over crumbling and crowded classrooms.

Riner, 37, who was born in the French Caribbean territory of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris, cited his years of throwing and pinning down judo opponents to make the case for being elected president. “Fighting has always been part of me. I know what it’s like to fight, fall and always get up,” he said. “France does not need a professional politician who recites lessons and quarrels all day long.”
In an interview with the newspaper Le Parisien published on Monday, he described his views as neither rightwing nor leftwing.

Instead Riner, one of France’s most recognisable and popular athletes, pointed to broader issues. “The country is experiencing deep divisions right now, let’s not kid ourselves,” he said. “And in the face of that, I don’t see a single candidate putting forward a credible and fair vision capable of bringing French people together rather than dividing them. There is no one today offering genuine, sincere hope. It’s always one side against another.”

As Riner prepared to attempt to gather 500 sponsorship signatures from elected officials, as required by French law, he said some of his motivation to run came from those young and old who were finding it difficult to envision a future for themselves.

“I hear the anger, which some people echo in their rhetoric with a great deal of negativity, coming from people who no longer have any ambition or the desire to think big,” he said. “Yet France is a great country. It allowed me to become the person I am today and gave me the opportunity to dream big. Today, that is precisely what is missing. There is no longer that ambition, no longer that hope.”
If elected, he said he was hoping to strike a balance between both careers so he would be able to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

He wouldn’t be the first judoka to embrace French politics: David Douillet was elected to the French parliament in 2009, years after his retirement from judo, later serving as the sports minister from September 2011 to May 2012.
Dani Podgoretskaya, an analyst at Eurasia Group, said there was little chance Riner would be seen as a serious contender.

“The French take the presidential election very seriously, given how much power the office holds. He has no experience in elected office, no party and no detailed programme yet,” she told Agence France-Presse. “While I still find it possible that we may yet see a providential figure emerge who unites the anti-populist vote, I doubt that Riner is that figure.”

When asked about his priorities on the world stage, Riner seized on the moment to crack a joke about potentially meeting the US president. “A lot of people around me have been talking about my first handshake with Donald Trump,” he said. With a laugh, he added: “We’ll see who has the firmer handshake.”

articles.title: Pat Conaty obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Charity executive helping people in poverty whose initiatives led to the foundation of National Debtline
body: My friend Pat Conaty, who has died aged 75, served for many years at the Birmingham Settlement, a charity that helps people in poverty and indebtedness. There, as development director, he pioneered a series of groundbreaking initiatives, including what became National Debtline, offering free support to people with debt problems in the UK.
In his work for Birmingham Settlement from the mid-1980s, Pat was seeing more and more people coming forward with debt problems, many of whom were victims of what he called “predatory lending”.

Witnessing first-hand the devastation wreaked by over-indebtedness, he led the collaboration with other debt advice agencies to establish in 1987 a phone line, together with a package of support material, to help people to help themselves. What began as a pilot advice service in Birmingham grew into National Debtline, now run by the Money Advice Trust.

In 1995, inspired by the community development bank, South Shore Bank, in Chicago, Pat led the establishment of the Aston Reinvestment Trust (ART), bringing together Adrian Cadbury as chair and Steve Walker, from Barclays, as chief executive, and working with Birmingham city council to develop a network of credit unions. ART advanced tens of millions of pounds to support local businesses and preserved thousands of jobs. Pat stayed in a development role with the trust, also initiating ART Homes to help people with the cost of home repairs.

Born in southern California, Pat was the son of Margaret (nee Gorman), a secretary, and Francis Conaty, a metallurgical engineer. He went to Junipero Serra high school in Gardena, then studied politics and economics at the University of California at Irvine and Riverside. After marrying a British woman, Rosemary Foggitt, in 1977, Pat moved with her the following year to the UK, settling in Birmingham.

Pat found work with Birmingham city council as a play leader before training as an adviser with Citizens Advice. In 1983 he joined Birmingham Settlement as a debt adviser, before becoming development director (1989-99). After a period of self-employment, Pat worked for New Economics Foundation (2003-08), then held an associate role at Co-operatives UK (2009-20).

In 2006 he moved to Powys to enjoy the peace of the Welsh countryside, but this did not stop his activism. He co-wrote The Resilience Imperative: Co-operative Transitions to a Steady-state Economy, with Mike Lewis (2012). In 2014 he was a founding director of the New Garden Cities Alliance in 2014. This interest was sparked by his own experience of bringing up children on a low income and looking for affordable housing in the 1980s.

He and I co-wrote two reports, Not Alone and Working Together (2017 and 2018), for Co-operatives UK and the Co-operative College, looking at how co-operatives can support the self-employed. The TUC also commissioned a handbook, Organising Precarious Workers (2017). In 2019 Pat was a founder member of union-coops:uk, a group working to get trade unions and worker co-ops to recognise their common aims.
Pat is survived by Rosemary, their daughter, Elsa, and son, Jake, and four grandchildren.

articles.title: Hometown glory? Norwegian library unveils £100k history book donated by Erling Haaland
articles.summary: Rare 16th-century edition of Viking royal sagas given to Bryne by Manchester City footballer and his father
body: At his local library in the southern Norwegian town of Bryne, the father of superstar striker Erling Haaland made a confession. “Sometimes my son and I are a little impulsive,” Alf Inge Haaland, known as Alfie, told the assembled crowd on Monday morning.

The spontaneous act in question was the purchase of the only surviving privately owned edition of a 1594 book, Snorre Sturlasons Kongesagaer (Snorre Sturlason’s Royal Sagas). The auction purchase for 1.3m Norwegian kroner (£103,000) was Norway’s most expensive ever book sale.

The Haalands then shocked and delighted their local librarian last December with the information that they planned to donate the exceptionally rare book to them so that it could go on permanent display in their home town.

The book was on Monday unveiled to an audience of excited schoolchildren at the Time library in Bryne. Many of the children are in the midst of a reading frenzy in the hope of winning a competition to see Haaland and his teammates play a match at the national stadium in Oslo.
“It’s a cool book with a lot of history,” the Manchester City and Norway striker’s father told the children. He also led a rendition of the Norwegian football team’s trademark Viking row with a drum.

His son, who could not be there in person, was shown in a video interview in which he talked about his interest in Vikings from a young age. Despite not being a big reader, he said that he did read a lot to his one-year-old son.

Snorri’s royal sagas chronicle the history of the Old Norse Viking and medieval kings of Norway, regarded by many Norwegians as a key document of national identity. The stories, about kings, queens, farmers and warriors, were first told orally and then written down by the Icelander Snorri Sturlason in the mid-13th century.

The book is the first printed edition of the sagas in Danish-Norwegian – Norway was under Danish rule between 1536 and 1814 – translated from the original Old Norse. At the time, there were no printing presses in Norway, so the edition was printed in Copenhagen and based on the translation of Mattis Størssøn.
The national librarian of Norway, Åse Wetås, said there were no known copies of the book like it. “It is a very special book for everybody in Norway.”

While they have three other copies at the National Library of Norway, none of them are complete. “This is a complete and very beautiful copy of this book from 1594,” she said. “There are some other copies, a few, but we don’t know any of them to be in this good condition. So it is a gem really. A very special gem.”
The book will be on public view in a display case at the library in Bryne and a digitised version of the full text is also available with explanatory notes.

Wetås said the gift was unlike anything she had ever come across and was especially important at a time when reading, writing and democracy were in crisis. “I think that’s the most important and long-lasting part of this: promoting reading, knowing your own history, promoting reliable sources.”

Haaland mania hit fever pitch in Bryne over the summer, when the 26-year-old Norwegian, who was born in Leeds where his father played for Leeds United, led his team to the World Cup quarter-finals. Their record-breaking run inspired visitors from across Norway and the world to visit the town in which he grew up and trained. As well as providing Bryne with yet another Haaland tourist attraction, the gift of the Royal Sagas book has further deepened his relationship with his home town.

Andreas Vollsund, the town’s mayor and Haaland’s former schoolteacher, said Haaland had always been a star in Bryne, but this latest move with the book and reading competition was “next level”. “We now see how good a person Erling is, to do this for his home town. He doesn’t need to do this, he wants to do this.”

Anne Tjørhom Frick, the library director at Time, said she was elated to have the book in Bryne. “It is quite surreal really that someone from a municipality of 20,000 can make such an impact on people worldwide, but also that he remembers where he came from,” she said. “We have had people come here all summer saying: ‘Where is the book?’ But now it is finally here.”

The Haalands’ reading competition, which will measure time spent reading through November and January, had inspired avid participation by the local schoolchildren, she said. On Tuesdays, when school closes at 1pm, she said pupils arrived 15 minutes later to start reading and did not leave until closing time at 6pm. Many of them, she said, “read in almost complete silence, only getting up to go to the bathroom or pick a book”.

articles.title: Polish prosecutors say ‘too early’ to tell if Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology
articles.summary: Terrorism investigation will continue after suspect who killed six after opening fire in market square died
body: Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man who killed six people and injured 16 in a rare mass shooting in Kraków to any particularly political ideology.

The 24-year-old Polish national died in hospital early on Monday after being critically injured in a shootout with police officers as they apprehended him after the attack in the city’s busy market square on Saturday afternoon.

Soon after the attack, the bodies of the gunman’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said on Saturday that the gunman, named in multiple reports as Michał Oksiński, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation, which the justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said would continue despite the gunman’s death and would aim to establish if he had acted alone or had been inspired by any group.
However, at a press conference on Monday, prosecutors said there was no evidence tying the suspect to any particular political bent.

“We do not have findings that we could, in a responsible way, categorically state that he was inspired by any particular ideology,” said the national prosecutor’s office spokesperson, Przemysław Nowak.
“It is far too early to comment on the motives … We have not found any obvious symbols that are generally associated with a particular political movement, whether far right or far left,” he added.
An interior ministry spokesperson told Polish radio that the “many emblems and patches” on Oksiński’s clothing were being analysed as part of the investigation.
Żurek also called for “restraint” earlier on Monday amid the ongoing investigation. “Evidence is ​being collected, ​but I will not ​show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” he told Radio ‌Zet.

Wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.

The shooting has shocked a country that had been considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.
Among the six victims were a 32-year-old British man and an Austrian woman aged 51. The other four victims were Polish nationals.

Of the 16 injured, 15 were in a stable condition as of late on Sunday, including two police officers who were brought out of medically induced comas earlier in the day. Five of the injured were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Police said the suspect, who had no criminal record and held a firearms licence, initially continued shooting even after he was wounded by police during the exchange of fire. The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties.
Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Mourners have left candles in tribute to the victims in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast during two days of national mourning, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

articles.title: Dortmund police attacked as crowd storms kebab shop for €1 doner
articles.summary: Officers pelted with bottles, stones and fireworks as people try to get their hands on special introductory offer
body: Police were called to a doner kebab shop in Dortmund, western Germany on Sunday after hundreds of customers stormed the premises in the hope of securing a portion for a one-off rock bottom introductory price.
The owner of the outlet was forced to call the police after becoming overwhelmed by the crowds that turned up for its opening.
According to the owner, about 1,000 people were present. Police put the number at about 300.

The owner had advertised his €1 (£0.83) kebab offer in advance. The average price of a doner – marinated meat roasted on a rotisserie spit, sliced off and served with salad in pockets of warm flatbread or wraps – is usually around €7.50 to €9.

Until about 2020, the price had been betwen €3.50 to €4. The steep rise, largely the result of higher energy and food costs, has turned Germany’s most popular fast food – which is served more than 1.3bn times a year – into a palpable everyday symbol of the effects of inflation.
The owner hired private security guards to oversee the opening, but after they were quickly overwhelmed, he was forced to call the police when the situation got out of hand.
Officers were pelted with bottles, stones, fireworks, an electric scooter and a chair, a spokesperson said. Reinforcements were called, amounting to about 100 officers on the ground and a helicopter.

The head of Dortmund’s police, Tim Frommeyer, condemned the incident in a statement. “Anyone who uses violence, in this case once again against police officers, is not an adventure-seeking youth or a troublemaker, but a criminal,” he said.
He accused some participants of having been out to attack the police from the start, describing it as part of a pattern of behaviour recently seen at rallies and demonstrations.
Several people were arrested. One was found to have a blank-firing pistol in his possession. A number of people face charges of breaching the peace, property damage and insult.
Police did not say whether the shop owner would face prosecution. He said he would donate the remaining kebabs to a homeless charity in the city.

The doner is seen as an immigrant success story, having been adapted into a flatbread snack by Turkish Gastarbeiter or guest workers in West Berlin more than 50 years ago. But a row erupted between Germany and Turkey two years ago when Istanbul applied to the European Commission to have the term recognised as a “guaranteed traditional speciality” throughout Europe.

Berlin objected and filed a veto, claiming the application would create large bureaucratic hurdles and lead to even more doner inflation through the introduction of strictly designated production methods and specifications for the meat and spices used, and even the types of knives used to cut it.
The Istanbul-based International Döner Federation formally withdrew its application last autumn.

articles.title: KFC’s arrival at Italian ski slopes angers food and mountain purists
articles.summary: Fast-food outlets at two prestigious Dolomites resorts are Italy’s first, with legal action threatened
body: Skiers on the slopes of two of Italy’s most prestigious resorts will be able to dine from buckets of fried chicken between runs this winter as the US fast-food chain KFC prepares to open outlets, infuriating mountain and food purists while prompting a prominent businessman to threaten legal action.

KFC will open its first high-altitude restaurants on the slopes of Cortina d’Ampezzo and Madonna di Campiglio, in the Dolomites, on 5 December, an initiative the company said was aimed at “surprising people” and “reaching places” where nobody would expect to find it.

The move marks a debut for any fast-food outlet on an Italian ski slope, bringing a menu replete with KFC’s most popular products, from spicy wings and burgers to traditional buckets of fried chicken.

The plans appear to have taken people by surprise, not least Alberico Zardini, a majority shareholder in Faloria Spa, the company that manages the infrastructure on Mount Faloria in Cortina d’Ampezzo, where there is to be a KFC at 2,123 metres.

“The mere idea is disgraceful,” Zardini told Il Messaggero. “It’s absurd and shameful to imagine a fast-food joint in the most beautiful spot in Cortina. Do the people of Cortina not realise what we’re risking here?”
Zardini said he had written to the bosses of Faloria warning that he would pursue legal action unless they put the brakes on KFC’s mountain ambitions.

He said it was “a mad decision”, especially because the outlet would be selling fried chicken inside the Faloria mountain club, where a luxury lodge is due to open on an upper floor. “I am 100% against it and will not just sit back and watch,” he said.
The KFC in Madonna di Campiglio, in south-western Trentino on the opposite side of the Dolomites, will be at 1,700 metres on Piana di Nambino, next door to a swish après-ski club.

The two outlets came under the fast food chain’s “quick service restaurants” product range and were the company’s way of targeting a broader market beyond its loyal Gen Z customers, “from young families to mountain lovers”, said Marzia Farè, the chief marketing officer for KFC Italia.

“We strongly wanted this project because it perfectly represents the way we imagine the evolution of KFC: continuing to surprise, reaching places where no one would expect to find us, and doing so without giving up what makes us unique,” she told brandnews.it.
Needless to say, with the cost of ski passes in Italy increasing each year, the outlets will appeal to those looking for cheap food in otherwise extremely pricey resorts.

But Oscar Farinetti, the founder of Eataly, Italy’s high-end food-store chain, has said the brand “doesn’t belong here at all” – while pointing the blame at customers. “We Italian consumers should be a tad more cultured,” he told Il Sole 24 Ore. “We need to acknowledge our assets – our cuisine made of few ingredients and excellent products. There is a lack of studying one’s own roots – we’re eating fried chicken instead of a nice slice of salami with a glass of fresh wine.”

Luigi Casanova from Mountain Wilderness, an NGO that works to protect mountain environments, told Corriere della Sera: “The era of polenta and luganega sausage is over,” while Paola Demagri, from Trentino’s provincial council, spoke about mountain identity being “sold out to Kentucky chicken”.

Others were more measured in their response. Cristian Ferrari, the president of Società Alpinisti Tridentini, the oldest mountain association in the Trentino area, said: “We have nothing against fried chicken, but are we sure this is the issue we should be most worried about?”
